body.hook: Artists rarely start with a perfect idea. Picasso made dozens of sketches for "Guernica." The sketchbook is where messy ideas get tested, changed and turned into something worth making.

study.title: From Prompt to Plan
study.question: How do artists turn a simple prompt into a strong idea?
study.passage:
Prompt: "Something I carry" (an object, a memory, a responsibility or a feeling).
Part 1, Mind map (10 minutes): Write the prompt in the centre of a sketchbook page. Branch out with at least 15 words, objects, places, people and feelings. Circle three that surprise you.
Part 2, Visual research (10 minutes): Collect references: draw two objects from life, take or find two photos, and note one artist who works with a similar idea.
Part 3, Thumbnails (15 minutes): Draw six thumbnails (5 cm by 7 cm) showing different compositions: close-up, bird's-eye view, unusual crop, symbolic object, combined images, empty space.
Part 4, Develop (10 minutes): Choose the strongest thumbnail. Make a larger study testing value or colour.
Part 5, Reflect (5 minutes): Annotate the page: Why this idea? What will you change? What feeling do you want the viewer to have?
study.source: Original studio task written for this lesson.

body.objective: Students will be able to create an expressive artwork.
body.iCan: I can create an expressive artwork.
successCriteria: I can use colour, line, mark-making and distortion to express a feeling
I can develop a sketchbook idea into a finished expressive artwork

body.hook: Edvard Munch's "The Scream" doesn't show what a person looks like. It shows what anxiety feels like. Expressive art uses colour, line and distortion to make feelings visible.

vocabulary.definition: Showing feelings or ideas through art.
An early 20th-century movement that distorted form and colour to express emotion.
Changing shapes or proportions on purpose for effect.
The different lines, dots and textures an artist makes.
Colour chosen for meaning rather than realism.
Energetic, expressive marks showing movement or emotion.

study.title: Make Feelings Visible
study.question: How do artists express emotion through visual choices?
study.passage:
Part 1, Look (10 minutes): Compare Munch's "The Scream" (1893), Van Gogh's "The Starry Night" (1889) and an Emily Carr forest painting. How do line, colour and distortion show feeling?
Part 2, Mark-making warm-up (10 minutes): Fill a page with six boxes labelled calm, anger, joy, fear, loneliness, excitement. Fill each with marks only (no pictures). Compare with a partner: can they guess the emotion?
Part 3, Create (35 minutes or across classes): Take your strongest sketchbook concept from the last lesson. Plan three deliberate choices: (1) a colour scheme chosen for symbolic meaning, (2) a type of mark-making, (3) one distortion (stretched shapes, exaggerated scale, tilted space). Make the final artwork in any 2D medium (paint, oil pastel, mixed media).
Part 4, Check (5 minutes): Ask a classmate what feeling they get, without explaining. Does it match your intent?

body.objective: Students will be able to write an artist statement.
body.iCan: I can write an artist statement.
successCriteria: I can explain the purpose of an artist statement
I can write a clear, concise statement about my artwork

body.hook: Next to every artwork in a gallery is a small block of text. In 100 words or so, the artist statement tells viewers what the work is about and why it was made, without explaining away the mystery.

vocabulary.definition: A short text explaining an artwork's idea, process and intent.
What the artist hoped to communicate.

study.title: In My Own Words
study.question: How do artists explain their work in a clear statement?
study.passage:
An artist statement answers: What is the work about? (concept) How did I make it? (materials and process) Why these choices? (intent) Sometimes: what do I hope viewers feel or think?
Model statement (original): "Weight. Acrylic and collage on board, 2026. My backpack has carried me through ten years of school. In this painting, I stacked collage papers from old tests and timetables until the backpack seems ready to burst, and painted the background in a cramped, cool palette. I distorted the straps to stretch across the whole surface, so the viewer feels the pull. I want the viewer to think about what young people carry, and what we might put down." (90 words)
Tips: first person, present tense, specific details, 75–150 words, avoid "I just liked it" and long technical lists, don't tell viewers exactly what to feel.
Activity 1 (10 minutes): Read two statements, one vague and one specific. List differences.
Activity 2 (20 minutes): Draft your statement for your expressive artwork.
Activity 3 (15 minutes): Peer feedback: highlight one sentence that helps you understand the work and one that's vague. Revise.
Activity 4 (5 minutes): Read your final statement aloud next to your artwork.
